new_statements.quote: this resulted in vowel-final lexemes that systematically received primary stress on their penultimate syllable, and secondary stress every second syllable leftward (e.g., *ˌsaŋaˈpulu). [...] The loss of word-final posttonic vowels explains why, in essentially all the languages of the area, words are now systematically stressed on their final rather than their penultimate syllable (contra Lynch 2000:77). Exactly the same evolution is attested in modern French: due to the progressive loss of all etymological posttonic vowels, French has become a perfectly oxytone language.

new_statements.rule_in_words: In the modern Torres-Banks languages, Lemerig among them, word stress falls on the final syllable: the Proto-Oceanic penultimate-stressed vowel became the last surviving vowel once post-tonic vowels were lost (*máte > mat), so the historically stressed syllable is now word-final.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated only for the proto-stage: 'secondary stress every second syllable leftward' from the penult (trochaic, right-aligned). Nothing said about secondary stress in modern Lemerig.
new_statements.exceptions: The rule is hedged as holding in 'essentially all the languages of the area'; the exceptions are not named. Mota is the evident exception (it kept final vowels, *mate > mate, sec. 3.2 p. 451). Lemerig lost all post-tonic vowels (Table 4 p. 476: 'loss of posttonic V2? all'), so the final-stress outcome applies to it.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress ('words are now systematically stressed'), stated areally for the 17-language corpus in a historical-phonology article, not as a Lemerig-specific synchronic description; no discussion of citation forms, phrase stress, or the prosody of prefixed article + noun (except the 2007 remark that the article carries no primary stress).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog leme1238 = ISO 639-3 [lrz] Lemerig, created 2009 by ISO change request 2008-069 (François) splitting the former [vlr] 'Vatrata' into Vera'a [vra] and Lemerig [lrz]. The Ethnologue 'dialects' Leon, Pak (Bek/Päk) and Sasar are earlier varieties of Lemerig; Codrington 1885's 'Pak' and 'Leon and Sasar' sketches therefore describe Lemerig varieties (and are silent on accent). François's modern data (2-3 last speakers, Päk variety mainly) underlie all the statements quoted here; the 2005 stress statement is areal (17 Torres-Banks languages), not specific to Lemerig.

sources.locator: p. 451, section 3.1 'Prosodic stress and vowel reduction' (Lemerig listed as LMG in Table 1 p. 445 and Table 4 p. 476)
sources.note: Sec. 3.1 p. 451: proto-forms had penultimate primary stress and secondary stress every second syllable leftward; after loss of word-final post-tonic vowels 'in essentially all the languages of the area, words are now systematically stressed on their final rather than their penultimate syllable (contra Lynch 2000:77)'. Lemerig (LMG) is one of the 17 languages (Table 1 p. 445) and lost all post-tonic vowels (Table 4 p. 476), so falls under the rule; no Lemerig-specific synchronic stress statement.

sources.citation: François, Alexandre. 2007. Noun articles in Torres and Banks languages: Conservation and innovation. In Siegel, Lynch & Eades (eds), Language description, history and development, 267-280. Amsterdam: Benjamins.
sources.note: Grep only: single remark that the noun article 'lacks its own primary stress, being prosodically integrated' to the noun; no Lemerig stress-placement statement.

sources.citation: Codrington, Robert H. 1885. The Melanesian Languages. Oxford: Clarendon Press. Sketches 'Pak' (pp. 333-336) and 'Leon and Sasar, Vanua Lava' (pp. 337-341).
sources.note: Pak and Leon/Sasar sketches (= Lemerig varieties) give alphabet and morphology only; no accent statement. The only Banks-Islands accent paragraph is for Mota (pp. 253-254: 'It cannot be said that the accent usually falls on any one syllable, except in words of two syllables, in which the stress is on the first').
11-vowel inventory (after François 2011 / Pangloss); no information on stress or accent.

sources.citation: François, Alexandre. 2021. Presentation of the Lemerig language and audio archive. Pangloss Collection, CNRS (Lemerig corpus page, 'Notes on the language').
sources.note: Orthography, 15 consonants, 11 vowels (Tables 1-2), pronouns; nothing on stress or prosody.

sources.citation: François, Alexandre. 2014. Structures et dynamiques des systèmes linguistiques: documentation, description, comparaison des langues océaniennes. Mémoire d'habilitation, INALCO, Paris.
sources.note: Lemerig vowel system (11 vowels i ɪ ɛ æ a œ ø ɔ ʊ u + ɒ̝; Fig. 15-16, pp. 84-85); vowel reduction described as syncope of atonic vowels from an ancestral right-aligned trochaic pattern *ˌCVCVˈCVCV (pp. 43-44, Mwotlap); no statement of Lemerig stress placement.

sources.citation: François, Alexandre. 2011. Social ecology and language history in the northern Vanuatu linkage: A tale of divergence and convergence. Journal of Historical Linguistics 1(2): 175-246.
sources.note: Sec. 4.2.1 pp. 193-194: vowel inventories grew 'via a historical process of metaphony, akin to umlaut, correlated with stress (François 2005a). A former trochaic foot *CV1CV2 regularly yielded a closed syllable CV'C'; Lemerig example *ndamu > tœm 'yam'. Nothing on synchronic stress placement.
